title: Trump Administration Appeals Ruling That Froze the $100,000 H-1B Fee
excerpt: The October 9 filing asks the Ninth Circuit to revive agency memos implementing the fee, which two federal judges have blocked and which employers currently do not have to pay.
body:
• The Trump administration on October 9 appealed to the Ninth Circuit to overturn a California ruling that froze the $100,000 fee on hiring H-1B workers from abroad.
  • The fee is currently not being collected: a Massachusetts court vacated the policy in June, and the First Circuit refused in July to pause that ruling.
  • For now, employers can file H-1B petitions without the $100,000 charge, though standard USCIS filing fees still apply.
  • DHS has separately proposed a permanent fee of about $103,000 through formal rulemaking, which has not taken effect.

Administration takes the fee fight to the Ninth Circuit

The Trump administration has asked a federal appeals court to overturn the California ruling that blocked its $100,000 charge on businesses hiring H-1B workers from outside the United States, according to Bloomberg Law. The appeal, filed October 9 with the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, targets the September 30 order by Judge Haywood S. Gilliam Jr., which barred US Citizenship and Immigration Services and Customs and Border Protection from enforcing the memos and guidance they issued to implement the fee.

Judge Gilliam found the agencies had implemented the policy without the notice-and-comment rulemaking the Administrative Procedure Act requires. His order covers both President Trump's original September 2025 proclamation and the extension issued last month, Presidential Proclamation 11069, which sought to run the fee through September 21, 2027.

Two courts have now blocked the fee

The California case, brought by a coalition of healthcare providers, universities, manufacturers, unions and individual workers, is the second legal defeat for the fee. In June, a federal judge in Massachusetts vacated the policy entirely in a challenge brought by 20 states, finding the administration lacked authority to impose the charge in that form. On July 24, the First Circuit declined to stay that ruling while the government's appeal proceeds, so the vacatur remains in force.

A third challenge, led by the US Chamber of Commerce, is pending before the DC Circuit after a district judge declined to enjoin the fee last year. The result is a patchwork in which the fee exists on paper but cannot be collected.

"Indian nationals bore a disproportionate share of the harm from this $100,000 fee, which put employment opportunities and families' futures at risk."

— Kalpana V. Peddibhotla, South Asian American Justice Collaborative

What this means for Indian professionals

The stakes are highest for Indians, who accounted for 71 percent of approved H-1B petitions in fiscal 2024, according to USCIS data cited in the litigation, with China a distant second at about 12 percent. The fee never applied to workers already in the US switching status, such as recent graduates, but it effectively priced out most hiring from abroad for hospitals, research universities, schools and smaller employers.

Practical position today: employers filing new H-1B petitions for workers outside the US do not owe the $100,000 charge while the court orders stand, but they should expect USCIS to move to collect it if an appeals court lifts the blocks — the agency has said DHS intends to collect the payment if the applicable order is lifted. Separately, DHS published a proposal in August for a permanent fee of roughly $103,000 on many cap-subject petitions, going through the formal rulemaking the courts found missing the first time. Petitioners can track case developments through USCIS and the Bloomberg Law case coverage.

What happens next

The Ninth Circuit will set a briefing schedule on the California appeal while the First Circuit considers the Massachusetts case on the merits. Either ruling could be appealed to the Supreme Court. Until an appeals court rules, the fee stays frozen — but the parallel DHS rulemaking means employers should plan for a version of the charge to return in 2027 even if the proclamation-based fee ultimately falls.
